cells.tense: You are at the table now, able to tell what matters and acting on it.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: That one you've been hauling past its finish — close it. Say where it really stands, set it down, and put the freed hour onto whatever is still growing.
cells.core:
You can pick out which of these things deserves the time before you've built a case for it, and the pick holds once the reasons arrive. What you tend gets your hands on it, not just your watchfulness, which is why the things around you are in decent shape. Finished and unfinished stay sorted in your head. Choosing a thing is how you can leave it at the end without feeling cheated.

So close out one thing properly. Take something you've been hauling past the point it was done, or something one push from finished, and finish it. Say plainly where it stands, then set it down. Give the hour that frees to whatever is still growing. What's complete doesn't need you standing over it. Letting go stops feeling like a loss once you've actually done it.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what matters here, and act like it.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them with your own hands.
cells.place: Where you can tell what matters before you can say why.

cells.tense: You will be further along a road you're already braced against.
cells.act: dream the next step and take it
cells.ask: Do the plainest thing the work is asking for, before you can picture how it lands. Nothing planned after that.
cells.core:
You can see the next three versions of what you're tending, and each one is harder to pin down, so nothing here gets finished long enough to count. Every project turns into a rehearsal for the real one. You learn well — you study how growth works, you take notes — and the studying is what keeps you one step back from the growing.

Borrow from the other side: sense one thing that hasn't happened yet, only that one. What is the material itself asking for, the plain next move? Do that, before you can see how it turns out, and don't plan the move after it. Handling the real thing, badly and briefly, will teach you more than a year of watching it. The brimming is the learning. Some of it has to spill.

cells.tense: You knew what mattered back then, standing at a door already closed behind you.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin a tray of seeds, or a first page, or ten minutes of something nothing depends on. No outcome attached, no reason needed.
cells.core:
You could tell what mattered here, and you could tell it early. That knowing is still around, and there's no grip on it now. Things get tended that don't get looked at — you tend the same pots out of habit, you keep the routine moving, and nothing new comes near the table. The room is cared for and vacant. Part of you hasn't arrived in it, so the hands stay busy while the person is somewhere else.

Don't try to feel your way back in first. Begin something that nothing is riding on, with no plan attached, and make the starting itself the point. A pot, a seed tray, a first page. Nothing hangs on whether it works. Doing it teaches you what no amount of deciding will, and the doing is what brings you back into the room where you used to be sharp.
cells.sheetLine: You knew then. The room's kept, waiting on you.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them with your own hands.
cells.place: Where you can tell what matters before you can say why.

cells.tense: You can name what matters here without noticing whose knowledge is doing the naming.
cells.act: drop one condition you set and take the step
cells.ask: Pick one condition you've set before something counts as finished — a tidy room, a good hour, a full page — and start the work without it.
cells.core:
You can tell what matters here, and you have a gift for handing that knowledge away. When it's clean, you know exactly which of these things deserves the time, then you file it under circumstance, or the situation, or the fact that anyone would have seen it. The judgment is yours, and it goes unsigned. The things you tend have been leaning on that judgment for a while now, whether or not your name is on it.

This week, choose one condition you've set before something counts — a quiet morning, a clean surface, the right version — and start on the work before it arrives. Notice afterward whose decision it was. You'll hear it in the plain sentence where you did the picking. A hundred hands lean on one person's sense of timing. It can have a name.

attempts.check: The draft keeps wanting to say the person has always known and always been wise — the record supports only that knowing-what-to-attend-to is the capacity this seat runs, not that they have it, use it, or were born to it. A reader could fairly say the steadying between two possible deadlines is just plain indecision, so the Balanced core names the act and not the person's nature. The Too Little read may be wrong about what emptied the room; the ask survives that, since starting one small unneeded thing is worth doing even if nothing is missing. The sentence that serves me more than them was a line about 'the room already knowing you' — cut, because it flatters the writing, not the reader. Too Much and Too Little are held as opposite failures: one runs ahead of the material, one has stopped entering it.
